issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident in a combat pilot, the threat profile should more plausibly center on accident recurrence, mechanical failure, bodily vulnerability, or generalized hypervigilance. 'Watching others closely for signs that they might harm me' implies an interpersonal assault/paranoia-like threat that is not supported by the trauma type or by the other selected items.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal set otherwise reflects post-traumatic identity disruption and emotional numbing ('Lost Emotions', 'Identity Loss'). 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is comparatively more characteristic of interpersonal violation or severe dissociation/depersonalization. In this profile it sits awkwardly with the accident trauma and with the other appraisal items, reducing thematic coherence of the node.

vignette:
Marcus was fifty-four and had spent thirty years in the cockpit of a fighter jet—first for his home nation in Oceania, then as a contractor for the U.S. Air Force. The accident happened on a clear afternoon during a routine training sortie over the Nevada desert. A catastrophic engine failure at fifteen thousand feet. He managed to eject seconds before the aircraft became a fireball, but the chute deployment was violent and he came down hard on a rocky ridge, fracturing three vertebrae and rupturing a disc in his lower back. Physically, he recovered over eighteen months. What did not heal, he came to believe, was something inside him.

In the months that followed, Marcus felt as though a vital part of himself had been sheared away. He could no longer recall what it felt like to be moved by anything—a sunset, his wife’s laughter, the roar of afterburners. “I will never feel normal emotions again,” he told himself, and the certainty of it lodged in his chest like shrapnel. He stared at his face in the mirror and barely recognized the man who had once been decisive, fearless, quick to grin. I don’t know myself anymore. And worse: I have permanently changed for the worse. These were not passing thoughts; they became the bedrock of his inner life, the filter through which every experience passed.

Because he believed he was fundamentally broken, Marcus began to treat the world as a place that could break him further. He started scanning every room for exits before he could sit down—the mess hall, the briefing room, even his own living room. At the base, he found himself walking the perimeter of the hangar during preflight checks, noting every emergency egress door, every fire extinguisher. He told himself it was professionalism, but the compulsion was relentless. At home, he could not sit with his back to a doorway. His wife, Lani, watched him jerk his head toward every unexpected sound—a car door, a creaking floorboard. He felt perpetually on guard, even inside his own four walls, as though the accident had left him with a radar that could never be switched off. Being superalert, watchful, on guard—that was his constant state. And the more he stayed on guard, the more it confirmed that he was indeed a changed, damaged man.

The connection tightened into a loop. Because he believed he had lost his core self and could not trust his own reactions, he had to monitor every potential threat. And because he was always monitoring, he never gave himself the chance to feel safe, which only deepened his conviction that his emotions were gone for good. At work, his escape-route planning became so obsessive that a younger pilot joked, “Marcus, you check the canopy release like it’s gonna save your life.” He did not laugh. What frightened him most was the certainty that this vigilance was necessary—that without it, he would be caught off guard, and that the next accident would finish what the first one started.

Months became years. Lani told him she felt as though she were living with a stranger who was always waiting for something bad to happen. He had withdrawn from their Saturday hikes, from barbecues with friends, from any situation where he could not mentally map an exit. She finally insisted he see a psychologist. He came to the appointment reluctantly, but he came. What he was hoping for, he admitted in the first session, was to feel less like a ghost. What he was most afraid of was that nothing could bring his old self back—that the man who had once flown into danger without a second thought was gone, and that all that remained was this watchful, hollow shell.
